1:
What the cloud is divides them at once. Gill hears an allusion to the Israelites encompassed by the pillar of cloud in the wilderness. Calvin denies the figure is scriptural at all: a cloud for a multitude is a classical metaphor, Homer having a cloud of footmen and of birds and Livy a cloud of horsemen — and he declines to take the word for witnesses in its usual sense of martyrs. Robertson agrees the word means a vast mass of cloud rather than a single one, and refers the picture to the great amphitheatre. Wesley calls them a multitude tending upward with holy swiftness. Calvin adds the argument from number: had they been few they ought still to have roused us, but a vast throng should stimulate us the more. Robertson protests at the printers, holding there should be no chapter division here, these verses being the climax of the whole argument.

Henry divides the duty into a preparatory part and a perfective one, and takes the weight as all inordinate affection for the body and the present life: such care is a dead weight on the soul, pulling it down when it should ascend and back when it should press forward, and making duty harder than it would be. The besetting sin he defines by advantage, the sin that has most of it against us from our circumstances and constitution. Wesley triples that — the sin of our constitution, of our education, of our profession — and reads the first clause from the racecourse, that runners throw off whatever damps the vigour of the soul. Ellicott, rendering the verse afresh, remarks that in one so difficult we need an exactness of translation not otherwise desirable.

On the looking they converge. Clarke says the verb means looking off and on, or from and to — off from the world and all secular concerns, and to Jesus — keeping the Grecian games in view, where runners held the mark in their eye. Robertson renders it looking away to Jesus, a glance at the cloud and then the eyes fixed on the goal. Gill insists the seeing is not with bodily eyes but with the eye of faith, at first glimmering and afterwards increasing. Wesley reaches for a type, our crucified Lord prefigured by the lifting up of the brazen serpent, our guilt by the stings, our faith by the Israelites' looking.

What the two titles make Christ is disputed. Barnes strikes out a word to settle it: our is not in the original and obscures the sense, Christ being first and last as an example of faith, not enumerated with those distinguished for it before but set above them all. Wesley reads the same two words the opposite way, of one who begins faith in us, carries it on and perfects it. Ellicott takes origination as the principal thought in the first; Robertson notes the second appears to be a word the writer coined. Clarke moves Christ off the track altogether, allowing that the first title generally means captain or leader but judging the reference here to be to the judge of the games, whose business it was to admit the contenders and award the prize. On the joy, Calvin prefers the sense instead of joy — it was free to Christ to exempt himself from all trouble, and he underwent instead a death bitter and in every way ignominious — while not much objecting if another takes the preposition of the final cause, that he refused not the cross because he saw its blessed issue. Robertson takes the exchange sense, the joy lying at the end of the race and the cross at this one, endured with contempt for a shame then attaching to the worst of deaths. Cyril of Jerusalem, on the sitting that follows, gathers its testimonies from the Gospel, from Peter, and from three letters.
3:
The opening verb is read as an act of measurement. Robertson calls it an old word meaning to reckon up, compare and weigh, found only here in the New Testament, and says understanding Jesus is the key to the whole problem and the cure for doubt. Ellicott renders it literally as compare: place your sufferings by the side of his. Wesley puts the comparison as a question — the Lord bore all this, and shall his servants bear nothing? Clarke asks more, that they analyse every part of Christ's conduct, enter into his spirit and examine his motives, remembering that as he acted they are called to act. Calvin states the argument formally: if the Son of God, whom all must adore, willingly underwent such conflicts, who should dare refuse the same — and one thought alone ought to conquer every temptation, that we are associates of the Son of God, who was so far above us and came down willingly to our condition. Gill takes the considering more widely, of the greatness of his person and his offices as prophet, priest and King.

What the sinners did is disputed on lexical grounds. Ellicott insists the word need not be limited to words, since the Greek Old Testament so often uses it of Israel's rebelliousness, and prefers to render it gainsaying. Robertson keeps it to the word itself, noting it has already appeared twice in the epistle. Barnes fills it out historically as the opposition of the Jews of the Saviour's time, who thwarted his plans, perverted his sayings and ridiculed his claims. Clarke adds the manner of the victory, that Christ bore continual opposition but conquered by meekness, patience and perseverance.

At the next verse the figure changes, and they disagree about what it changes into. Ellicott says the contest of the pugilists is substituted for the footrace — in the first verse sin was the hindrance to be put aside, here the antagonist to be subdued — and notes the same transition in the Corinthian letter. Clarke agrees, calling it an allusion to boxing at the Grecian games. Robertson takes the verb off the sand altogether: it means to stand in opposition in a line of battle, a compound found only here. On the substance they agree. Barnes reads a plain comparison of degree, that great as their trials seem their faith has not been put to the severest test, so they ought not to yield. Clarke says many already named were martyrs who sealed the truth with their blood, which these readers have not been called to do. Gill lists what they had resisted — sin, Satan, the world and its frowns and flatteries, the false teachers — but not blood, as some of the old saints had, and some in the times of the Maccabees, and James, and Christ himself. Henry concedes the other side first, that they had suffered much and striven to an agony, and defends the warfare as honourable and necessary, since we defend ourselves against what would destroy us if it won.

Calvin then finds the one place where the comparison with Christ breaks. Even when the ungodly persecute us for Christ's sake, he says, we are contending against sin — and into that contest Christ could not enter, being free from all sin; in this we are unlike him, for sin always dwells in us and afflictions serve to put it to flight. Chrysostom, standing further back, observes that two kinds of consolation are used at once which look opposed yet lend each other strength: the one saying a man has suffered much, since the soul is refreshed when it has many witnesses of its sufferings, which is why the former days were recalled; the other saying he has suffered little.
5:
Three turn the opening clause into a question. Calvin reads it so outright, holding that the asking intimates it was not yet time to forget; Gill allows the same; Clarke prints it as a question too. Wesley keeps the indicative, softened: they seem already to have forgotten. Clarke draws a conclusion about the speaker: the words in Proverbs, which at first sight seem to come from Solomon to his son, are properly from God himself to anyone in distress. Ellicott prefers to render the verb as holding converse, or reasoning, with them as with sons, and notes the citation follows the Greek except that son becomes my son and reproveth becomes chasteneth. Barnes states its purpose, that afflictions were designed to produce happy effects and are therefore to be borne patiently; Calvin divides it in two, the injunction not to reject correction and the reason, that the Lord loves.

Whether that reason bears the weight is the sharpest question here, and Calvin raises it against himself. It seems not to be a well-founded reason, he says: God visits elect and reprobate indiscriminately, and his scourges manifest wrath oftener than love, as Scripture speaks and experience confirms — and he answers only that when the godly are addressed, the effect they feel is alone in view. Barnes takes it as a universal rule and guards it twice: it does not mean God sends chastisement undeserved, nor for the mere purpose of inflicting pain, which cannot be, but that by chastening he shows a paternal care. Gill narrows the premise instead: all men are not the objects of God's love, only a special people chosen in Christ and loved with an everlasting love. Clarke and Wesley draw the practical inference without the difficulty — it is a proof of fatherly love, so neither neglect the correction nor faint under it. Robertson remarks only that this is a hard lesson to learn.

At the next verse the dispute is what kind of condition is stated. Barnes insists it means not if you bear it patiently but if you are chastised at all, the affirmation relating to the fact and not the manner. Clarke reads exactly the manner Barnes excludes, of submitting to God's authority and humbling oneself under his hand; Gill likewise, of enduring in faith, with patience, courage, humility and reverence. Ellicott removes the condition altogether, reporting that the whole weight of ancient evidence favours a change in the first Greek word, yielding either that it is for chastening that they endure, or simply endure, for chastening — bearing the trial instead of escaping it by unworthy concession. Robertson accepts the same reading. Calvin argues from ordinary practice: no prudent man leaves his children uncorrected, since without discipline they cannot be led aright, so much less will God neglect so necessary a remedy.

The last verse turns the argument round, the harsh word being treated as an argument from social fact. Clarke says it proceeds on the observation that such children are neglected in manners and education, their fathers feeling little affection — and adds that the word for chastening does not imply stripes at all but the whole discipline of a child. Barnes puts it negatively: if nothing ever comes that is adapted to correct their faults or chide their wanderings, it would prove them cast off and disregarded. Ellicott states the inference as a bare impossibility, that if they had never known this chastening they are not sons whom a father acknowledges. Wesley adds the only qualification anyone offers, that all sons partake of it more or less. Ellicott has meanwhile made a second textual note, that the Hebrew as it stands yields even as a father the son in whom he delighteth, while a very slight change in one word gives the sense the Greek translators took — a difference he judges immaterial here.
9:
Ellicott marks the turn: the argument has run on likeness, that God chastens as a father, and here passes to contrast, between our natural parents and the Father of spirits, Creator of all spirits and Giver of life to all. Two of them press the phrase further than that. Gill takes fathers of the flesh to be so called because they are the immediate causes of their children's bodies, which shows the soul is not had from them; Wesley says the same more tentatively, that perhaps the expressions intimate our earthly fathers are parents of our bodies only, our souls not being derived from them. Calvin numbers the parts of the comparison: if we so reverenced the fathers from whom we descended after the flesh, much more honour is due to our spiritual Father; and their discipline is useful only for the present life, while God looks farther, to prepare us for an eternal one. Clarke concedes a fault, that we reverenced our natural parents notwithstanding that their corrections often arose from whim or caprice. Robertson notes the verb is an imperfect of customary action.

What the few days measure is answered four ways. Gill denies it refers to the minority of children or the short life of parents and makes it the end they aim at, their children's temporal good. Barnes makes it the reference of the correction to this short life. Clarke makes it duration and extends it: our parents' chastisement lasted a short time, and our Father's will also be short if we submit, since as they ceased when we learned obedience so will he when the end is accomplished — God delights not in the rod, and judgment is his strange work. Wesley makes it life itself, how few are all our days.

The second half of the contrast is about competence. Ellicott renders it as seemed good unto them, setting human liability to mistake against the knowledge of a Father who cannot err in the means he employs. Wesley states the fault plainly, that they erred by too much indulgence or severity, while he always acts for our profit. Barnes locates the difference in temper: in God everything is without intermingling of passion, whereas in an earthly parent much is the result of hasty emotion and an irascible disposition. Calvin locates it in the end, that God's chastisements mortify the flesh so that we may be renewed for a celestial life, a benefit not to be expected from men.

On the last verse the question is how wide the maxim runs. Ellicott, adopting a slightly changed reading, renders it that all chastening seems for the present not joyous but grievous, and holds the language perfectly general, of every chastening human or divine; Wesley agrees. Gill treats it narrowly, as anticipating an objection drawn from the grief afflictions bring, granting only that none seems joyous to flesh and blood. Calvin gives the reason for the concession, that we should not measure God's chastisements by present feeling, being like children who dread the rod because their age cannot yet judge how useful it may be. Barnes refuses to soften the pain: chastisement is intended to produce it, and the Christian is as sensitive as others, religion not blunting his sensibilities into stoicism but increasing his susceptibility — the Lord Jesus himself probably feeling reproach and contempt more keenly than any. Clarke widens the field to correction, restraint, domestic regulation and gymnastic discipline, none pleasant, yet the means by which obedient children, scholars and great men are made. Chrysostom compares the orders: those who drink bitter medicines first submit to unpleasantness and afterwards feel the benefit, and so with virtue and vice — in vice the pleasure first and the despondency after, in virtue the reverse — but there is no equality, since to be first grieved and then pleased is not the same as the opposite.
12:
Whose limbs are meant is not agreed. Gill takes the words as spoken to the Hebrews about themselves, noting a version reading your hands and your knees, and lists where the sluggishness showed — in prayer, in hearing the word, in holding fast their profession. Wesley allows both, whether your own or your brethren's. Ellicott makes the turn communal, the writer passing from personal duty to what is binding on all members of a body. Wesley divides the two members between the two figures already used, hands unable to continue the combat, knees unable to continue the race.

The verb is stronger than the English shows. Ellicott renders it make straight again, restore to a right state, and calls the clause almost a reproduction of the prophet; Robertson gives the same sense and parses the two participles as perfect passives, one of a verb meaning to relax, the other of one meaning to loosen at the side, to paralyse. Barnes reads the posture from life, the hands falling by the side when a man is exhausted with toil or worn by disease, and turns it into a summons to renew courage. Clarke describes people almost worn out with sickness and fatigue, whose knees shake, and assures them they shall infallibly conquer if they persevere. Henry grants the fact before the remedy, that affliction is apt to make the hands hang down and the knees grow feeble, and says that against this a man must strive. Calvin puts the cause further back: nothing discourages us more than to have no taste of God's grace in adversities, and nothing raises us more than knowing God is present even when he afflicts.

What making the paths straight requires is answered four ways. Barnes takes the word not as upright but as level and smooth, so that the duty is to remove every obstacle lest they stumble and fall, and Wesley agrees, adding that the paths are for your own and their feet alike. Clarke reads it as choosing between roads rather than clearing one: take the straight path and avoid the rough ways full of stones and briers by which you will be lamed, since in the even path what was wounded by a wrong turning will be healed by moderate exercise. Gill makes it a rule of doctrine, the word of God alone being the rule of walking. Calvin makes it prudence, stating the danger from the opposite side: indiscreet ardour is no less an evil than inactivity and softness. Robertson supplies the picture behind the noun, the track of a wheel, so that straight wheel-ruts are asked for; Ellicott traces the phrase to the Greek of Proverbs, where the verb means rather to make even than to ponder.

The closing clause is read medically by one and morally by another. Robertson notes the verb is an old one meaning to turn out, to twist, to put out of joint, and calls the sentence a vivid picture of concern for the lame. Wesley takes it of the weak, scarce able to walk, being turned out of the way of faith and holiness. Ellicott warns that the difficulty here is concealed when the clause is separated from what precedes, as the English does, since the Greek will not allow it. Clarke says the lamed traveller is totally prevented from proceeding, and Henry closes positively, that faith and patience enable believers to follow peace and holiness as a man follows his calling.
14:
The pursuit is taken literally. Clarke says the verb means to chase peace as beasts pursue their game, tracing it through all its winding circumstances — though he adds, with all men if you can with a safe conscience. Robertson gives the same image and adds that the whole world needs the lesson. How far all men reaches divides them. Barnes holds it must be understood mainly of persecutors, the readers' trials having arisen chiefly from that quarter. Ellicott insists the charge is general and must not be limited to fellow Christians, both admonitions being admirably suited to a time of persecution. Gill enumerates the relations and extends it to enemies. Calvin explains why the labour is needed: men are so born that all seem to shun peace, each studying his own interest, so that unless we strenuously labour we shall never retain it. Chrysostom puts the two graces above everything: many things are characteristic of Christianity, but more than all are love and peace, which is why Christ left his peace and made mutual love the mark of discipleship.

The next participle is an official word, and three say so. Gill notes it means acting the part of overseers, and asks whether the charge falls on the church's officers or on the members themselves, preferring the latter. Calvin observes the word properly means overseeing, whence the title of bishop, then lists six renderings before settling on taking heed. Robertson notes it occurs in the New Testament only here and in Peter. Barnes gives the reasons — our propensities to evil, the temptations of the world, the allurements to apostasy.

What the danger is gets three renderings. Ellicott prefers whether any one be falling back from the grace of God, adding that one member's defection brings loss and danger to the whole body. Clarke makes it falling off from this grace, by which he means the gospel system itself. Ellicott finds a passage of Deuteronomy plainly behind the root of bitterness though not formally quoted; Wesley names the roots — envy, anger, suspicion — then generalises, that any corruption may pollute many.

Whether Esau is charged with the first sin as well is disputed. Clarke denies it, since the disjunctive separates the two; Esau is called profane for disregarding the spiritual advantages of his birthright. Ellicott reports that Jewish tradition does affirm it but judges it improbable here, taking Esau as a type of those who care only for the gains and pleasures of this world. Barnes calls him corrupt as well as profane, and notes that many refer the first word to idolatry. Robertson glosses profane as trodden under foot, and finds the idea of exchange in the phrase about the meal. Gill turns to discipline, that such a person is not to be continued in the church's communion; Calvin to structure, the writer naming a particular defilement and passing to the general term. Cyril of Jerusalem applies the verse to an order, bidding the solitaries and virgins give heed first and the rest follow, since a great dignity must not be bartered for a petty pleasure.

On the repentance Esau could not find, Clarke says the word is not to be taken in a theological sense as implying contrition, and Robertson that it means a change of mind and purpose rather than sorrow. Wesley says there was no room for a repentance which would regain what he had lost, and that he sought too late. Barnes distinguishes the two things at stake: the blessing sought was not the birthright, which Esau knew he could not regain, but what the father pronounced on his eldest. Ellicott reaches the same by punctuation, making the clause a parenthesis that explains the rejection. Calvin gives the sequence of Esau's mind, that he first regarded the sale as a child's play and found only too late what a loss he had incurred.
18:
The comparison is introduced as an argument, and each says what for. Barnes calls it a sublime comparison enforcing what precedes, its object being to guard them against apostasy. Henry sets out the double point, how far the gospel church differs from the Jewish and how far it resembles the church in heaven, and calls the Mosaic state a gross sensible one. Calvin says the writer fights with a new argument, proclaiming the greatness of the grace made known by the Gospel and commending its benign character. Clarke insists the words should be rendered a palpable or material mountain, precisely because it was not one that might then be touched — the history forbids it and the apostle confirms it two verses later. Robertson notes there is no word for a mount in the Greek at all, though one is understood since the datives agree with it. Wesley glosses it as of an earthy, material nature.

The terrors are then itemised. Robertson traces the vocabulary: the word for blackness is a late form akin to the word for cloud, while the word for darkness is Homer's for the gloom of the world below. Barnes observes that the trumpet amid the tempest was fitted to increase the terror, and that it is easy to conceive what awe a voice must have produced which came from the midst of the storm yet was heard by hundreds of thousands. Ellicott supplies the words of the entreaty, that if they heard the voice of the Lord any more they should die. Wesley judges the trumpet was formed by the ministry of angels. Calvin puts the scene to one purpose, that when the Law was promulgated there was nothing but terrors on every side, to show that God had ascended his tribunal. Chrysostom grants the awe on both sides and marks the difference: wonderful were the things in the Temple and awful those at Sinai — but the New Covenant was not given with these.

What they could not endure divides two of them. Barnes says the commands themselves were not intolerable, but the manner of their communication inspired a terror they could not bear, since they feared they should die. Gill locates it in the law itself, and is careful to say it was not that they despised it as unregenerate men do, but that they could not bear it as a yoke of bondage nor as a covenant of works giving no strength to perform. Ellicott makes two editorial judgements: that there is no reason to enclose these verses in a parenthesis, and that the clause about being thrust through with a dart is absent from the best authorities and entered accidentally from Exodus.

The saying attributed to Moses raises a question of source. Barnes states it plainly: the words are not in the account of the giving of the law, and the apostle's authority for them has been questioned, though Moses says something like it in Deuteronomy after breaking the tables. Ellicott sharpens it: the Greek of that passage has part of the words, but on a later occasion. Gill does not raise it, taking the terrible sight as the smoke and fire, or as God himself, and citing a version reading that so terrible was he who vouchsafed himself to be seen. Wesley draws the point that matters: even Moses, admitted to so near an intercourse that God spoke to him as to a friend, stood while the ten words were pronounced not as mediator but as one of the hearers. Cyril of Jerusalem turns from the mountain to the incarnation — these things the Jews read but do not hear, having stopped the ears of their heart, whereas we believe in one who came in the flesh because we could not receive him otherwise: unable to look on him as he was, we needed him to become what we are.
22:
Whether the coming is present or future divides them. Gill takes Mount Sion and the names beside it for the church under the Gospel dispensation, to which the Hebrews had already come, and reports the variant in one copy which would favour the heavenly reading. Wesley denies exactly that: the apostle speaks not of the church militant but of the New Testament believer's communion with the church triumphant, far more apparent to celestial spirits than to our eyes, which are yet veiled. Ellicott insists on the literal Greek, unusually important in verses so difficult, and renders it Zion the mountain and city of a Living God, a heavenly Jerusalem; Jewish writings, he adds, often dwell on a celestial city the counterpart of the earthly, so the words were familiar. Robertson marks the sharp contrast with the earlier verse. Calvin hears the prophecies in which God promised his Gospel should go forth from Zion, and says the epithet heavenly is added so that the Jews should not cleave to what was earthly. Cyril of Jerusalem tells it as history, that after the Jews were cast away the Saviour built out of the Gentiles a second holy Church, of which he spoke in promising to build upon the rock.

The next word raises a question of punctuation. Clarke reports that some of the best manuscripts join it to what precedes, and several of the fathers quote it so — the general assembly of innumerable angels — which he judges probably the true connection. Robertson allows that connection as possible but not certain, and takes the church of the firstborn as a further item. On the sense they agree: Clarke derives it from the words for all and for assembly and takes it of a festive gathering; Gill describes the Greek usage at games, feasts and fairs; Wesley calls it a stated convention on a festival occasion.

Who the firstborn are is the third dispute. Calvin denies the title to God's children indiscriminately, reserving it as an honour for the patriarchs and renowned saints of the ancient Church; the enrolment he refers to God's having all the elect written in his book. Wesley opens it wide, to the whole body of true believers on earth or in paradise, and observes that where Israel's firstborn were enrolled by Moses these are enrolled in heaven — and that they stand nearer to God than the angels named before them. Barnes takes them as saints distinguished for piety, arguing from the pre-eminence the firstborn enjoyed among the Hebrews. Ellicott changes the following phrase, holding the Greek order requires a Judge who is God of all, and marks the turn: the thought has rested on those who have inhabited heaven from their creation, whereas men who have passed through this life have no essential right of citizenship there and come first before a Judge.

The last clauses are the summit, and they say so. Wesley says the gradation is here at its highest point, glosses the sprinkled blood as all the virtue of that blood by which we are sprinkled from an evil conscience, and sets it against Abel's, which cried for vengeance. Clarke states the succession, the old covenant and its mediator passed away while the new is in force to the end of the world. Ellicott finds a change in the Greek: elsewhere the word for new implies newness of kind, but here the covenant is one newly made. Robertson will not let the name pass unremarked: he is there as Lord and Saviour and still Jesus. Calvin explains why the clause comes last, since through him alone the Father is reconciled to us, so that we may come without fear; the phrase, after the Hebrew manner, means sprinkled blood. Gill adds what the coming is, by faith, not a corporeal coming in the days of his flesh nor an outward attendance on ordinances.
25:
Who is speaking is disputed. Gill takes it of Jesus, the Mediator whose blood was just named. Clarke says the same and completes the contrast: the one who now speaks from heaven by his Gospel is the Lord Jesus, the one who spoke on earth was Moses. Barnes and Ellicott make the speaker God in the gospel, Barnes adding that God has addressed them there as really as he addressed the Hebrews at Sinai. Ellicott notes the same verb is used twice of declining to listen, pointing back to the Israelites who deprecated hearing more words. Calvin observes the verb is the one used earlier of that entreaty but means something else here, that we must not reject the word destined for us. Robertson states the paradox the argument turns on: the consequences are dreadful to apostates now, for Zion has greater terrors than Sinai.

Whose voice shook the earth is a second question. Gill says Christ was present at the giving of the law and his voice was then heard; Clarke draws the same conclusion, that it seems to have been Jesus whose voice shook the earth and who came down on the mount, but records that others refer it simply to the Father. Ellicott makes the terrors of Sinai a type of a more terrible revelation, when earth and heaven shall both be moved and all that is transitory pass away. Calvin puts the comparison in degrees, that though God shook the earth when he published the Law he now speaks more gloriously, shaking both. Wesley balances the promise, joyful to the saints though dreadful to the wicked.

What the removal amounts to divides them. Clarke reads it historically, of the whole Jewish polity, shaken ever since Judea fell under Roman power, and takes the things made as subjects intended to last only for a time, God never having designed that religion to become general. Ellicott insists on the opposite scale: the phrase means once more only, and the words must of necessity point to the final change and the removal of everything that can pass away. Wesley identifies the things shaken as heaven and earth, made and therefore liable to change, so that what remains is the new heaven and earth. Calvin is most careful with the quotation: the prophet's words are yet a little while, meaning the calamity would not be perpetual, but the Apostle lays no stress on that expression and infers only from the shaking that the world's state was to change at Christ's coming.

The conclusion is drawn from the one thing that does not move. Barnes contrasts it with what went before, that this kingdom is not, like the Jewish dispensation, to give place to another. Clarke identifies it with the Gospel dispensation, in which God reigns among men and in the hearts of them that believe. Robertson calls the verse the ground of loyalty to Christ and renders the exhortation as continuing, let us keep on having grace. Wesley makes the receiving an act of willing and joyful faith, and glosses the reverence asked for as literally shame, from a deep consciousness of our unworthiness. Chrysostom sets the exhortation beside another of the same kind, that the things seen are temporal while the things not seen are eternal, from which the writer elsewhere draws comfort about present evils. Clarke draws the moral that sin under the Gospel is as abominable as under the law, and Ellicott notes that in Deuteronomy these words follow a warning against idolatry. Calvin marks the method rather than the matter: having kindly set before us the grace of God, the writer now makes known his severity, God beginning with love so that we may follow the more willingly. Gill keeps the two together in one person: Christ is truly God and our God, and though full of mercy will appear in wrath to his enemies.
